parole.testo: From earlier بَادِنْگَان (bādingān), an Indo-Aryan borrowing, from Sanskrit वातिङ्गण (vātiṅgaṇa), from Dravidian, ultimately from Proto-Dravidian *waẓVtV.
Borrowed from a descendant of Sanskrit बाण (bāṇa).
Ultimately from Sanskrit ब्राह्मण (brāhmaṇa).
Borrowed from Sanskrit त्रिपुटा (tripuṭā), त्रिपुट (tripuṭa), literally “triplicated”, names of several plants.
Possibly a metathesized and zetacized derivative of Sanskrit त्रपुस (trapusa, “colocynth fruit”) (compare خَربُز (xarboz)).

Related to Kermanic [script needed] (tü), Mazanderani [script needed] (tir), [script needed] (tīr), Khwarezmian [script needed] (twt), Wakhi tыt, tыẟ, Munji tūy, Northern Luri تیت (tit) Parachi tī, Waneci [script needed] (tūwa, təwā), Sanskrit तूत (tūta), तूद (tūda), Kashmiri तूल् (tūl), تُل (tul),

Ultimately from Sanskrit तुत्था (tutthā), although it actually means “copper sulphate“. Alternatively it is from a variant of دود (dud, “smoke”), in the pattern of مُومِیَا (mūmiyā) and بامیا (bāmiyā) and like Arabic دُخَان (duḵān, “smoke”).
* Borrowed from Sanskrit तुर (tura). * Corruption of/confusion with تانول (tânul) and نول (nul).

Related to Central Kurdish قاشقاشە (qaşqaşe), Pashto قشقاق (qašqâš), قاشقاش (qâšqâš), and further likely to Middle Armenian կակաչ (kakačʻ), Georgian ყაყაჩო (q̇aq̇ačo), Karachay-Balkar къачхач (qaçxaç), Kumyk шакъшакъ (şaqşaq), Abaza къвашвхӏа (qʷʼašʷḥa), East Circassian ӏущхьэ (ʼwuśḥɛ), Japanese 芥子
Ultimately from Sanskrit देवनागरी (devanāgarī).
Borrowed from Sanskrit राजन् (rājan).

Ultimately from Sanskrit रास्ना (rāsnā, “Rasna, Pluchea lanceolata”, literally “rope, girdle; string of medicinal or potent-tasting herbs”), used throughout Ayurvedic literature; another plant within the Asteraceae family just as Inula helenium.

parole.significato: teak tree and wood (Tectona gen. et spp.)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Sanskrit शाक (śāka, “vegetable; herb; teak-tree”).
Borrowed from Sanskrit सुरा (surā) from Proto-Indo-Iranian *súraH (“liquor”). Cognate with Avestan 𐬵𐬎𐬭𐬁 (hurā), Middle Persian [script needed] (hwl /⁠hur⁠/).

Ultimately from Sanskrit शिशुमार (śiśumāra, “alligator; river dolphin”), from शिशु (śiśu, “child”) + मार (māra, “killing”). سوس (sus, “(rare) lizard”) is a backformation from a reanalysis of the second element as مار (mâr, “snake”).
Borrowed from Sanskrit शालि (śāli, “rice”).
Derived from Sanskrit शृङ्ग (śṛṅga). Related to سرنا (surnā /sornâ).
Borrowed from Sanskrit शृङ्गवेर (śṛṅgavēra). Doublet of زنجفیل (zanjefil) and زنجبیل (zanjebil).

parole.significato: apron, towel, waistwrap (especially worn in baths)
parole.testo: From an Indian language, ultimately from Sanskrit पोत (pota, “cloth”). The spelling with ط is an orthographic reborrowing from Arabic فُوطَة (fūṭa).
Borrowed from Sanskrit कुलञ्जन (kulañjana), possibly from Chinese 高良薑／高良姜 (gāoliángjiāng).
Borrowed from Sanskrit निम्बू (nimbū), borrowed from an Austroasiatic language.

parole.significato: mung bean (Vigna radiata, ماشسبز (mâš-sabz)) and mungo bean (Vigna mungo, ماشسیاه (mâš-siyâh))
parole.testo: From or otherwise related to Sanskrit माष (māṣa, “mungo bean”).

parole.significato: the charmed circle of a conjuror
parole.testo: Ultimately from Sanskrit मण्डल (maṇḍala).
From Sanskrit.

Perhaps ultimately from Sanskrit मगध (magadha), the land of the Buddha, in reference to the people's Buddhist faith and their kings' claim of descent from Magadha. Compare Bengali মাঘ (magh, “Arakanese”), Bengali মগ (mog, “Arakanese”).
From Sanskrit नारङ्ग (nāraṅga, “orange tree”).
Borrowed from Sanskrit नारिकेल (nārikela, “coconut”).

parole.significato: cardamom (Seed of Elettaria cardamomum, used as a medicine and spice, especially in curry powder)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sanskrit एला (elā), borrowed from a South Dravidian language, from Proto-South Dravidian *ēlV- (“cardamom”).
Borrowed from Sanskrit वचा (vacā, “sweet flag”).
Borrowed from Sanskrit विहार (vihāra).
Borrowed from Sanskrit छत्त्र (chattra). Doublet of چادر (čâdor) and چتری (čatri).

From Middle Persian [script needed] (*kʾsk' /⁠kāsag⁠/) (compare Baluchi کاسگ (kāsag, “bowl”)), possibly from Old Persian 𐎣𐎠𐎿𐎣 (kāsaka, “semi-precious stone, glass”), or perhaps related to Sanskrit कोश (kośa, “pot, cask, cup”). Likely not related to Sanskrit काच (kāca, “glass”).
Borrowed from Sanskrit खण्ड (khaṇḍa).
